title: Annotatio I §.III GENERICA remote: Disparatum de disparato — Carlstadt Identica out; Gomarus / Bellarmine
pass_a_gloss: The GENERIC nature of this proposition (1) as remoter genus shows that a Disparate is predicated in it of a disparate — whether the subject τὸ hoc designates bread alone, or besides bread something else, namely Christ’s body itself — provided the Carlstadt Identica This Body is my body remain excluded and exploded, hateful to both Protestant parties by its novelty and fiction and by δισερημηνεία and violent tearing from its antecedents. For insofar as Christ’s body is predicated of bread, even if that bread has Christ’s body joined to itself, a disparate is certainly predicated of a disparate: But the nature of disparates predicated of each other, because they are disparates, brings in improper predication and rejects the proper; otherwise every improper predication is removed from the midst: For what things will be improperly predicated of each other, if not disparates? Certainly nothing can be said improperly of itself: nor can any metonymy or metaphor be given except in Disparates. This argument, if anyone else, the most learned Gomarus most acutely built and deduced, Theological Works Tom. 3, Disp. 35 from thesis 14 to 20 inclusive, ending at last in these words of Bellarmine: We have no need here of Aristotle, since common sense suffices. For if it be allowed to affirm disparates properly of disparates, it will be allowed by the same right to affirm something of nothing, nothing of something, darkness of light, light of darkness, Belial of Christ, Christ of Belial: nor does our faith oblige us to defend what imply contradiction, p. 139.
pass_b_english: As remoter genus, the GENERIC nature shows a disparate predicated of a disparate — whether τὸ hoc is bread alone, or bread with Christ’s body besides — once Carlstadt’s Identica This Body is my body is exploded as a novel fiction both Protestant sides hate.

Body predicated of bread is disparate of disparate; disparates force improper predication and shut out the proper — otherwise no improper speech would remain, and no metonymy or metaphor could exist except among disparates.

Gomarus builds this sharply (Tom. 3, Disp. 35, th. 14–20), ending with Bellarmine: common sense suffices — if disparates may be affirmed properly of disparates, one may as well affirm nothing of something, darkness of light, Belial of Christ (p. 139).
source_text: GENERICA propositionis hujus natura (1) quà genus remotius, ostendit, Disparatum, in ea, de disparato praedicari, sive subjectum, τὸ hoc, solum panem, sive cum pane aliud praetereà, ipsum scil. Christi corpus, designet, dummodo exclusa explosaque maneat Carlstadiana Identica: Hoc Corpus est corpus meum, uti novitate & fictione, ita δισερημηνείᾳ & violentâ ab antecedentibus suis discerptione, utrique Protestantium parti merito suo exosa. Quatenus enim corpus Christi de pane, junctum licet sibi corpus Christi habente, praedicatur, praedicatur utique disparatum de disparato: At disparatorum natura, de se invicem praedicatorum, eò quòd disparata sunt, praedicationem impropriam infert, propriam respuit; sin minus, omnis praedicatio impropria è medio tollitur: Quaenam enim de se impropriè praedicabuntur, si non disparata? Certè, quicquam de seipso non potest impropriè dici: nec ulla potest dari metonymia, aut metaphora, nisi in Disparatis. Argumentum hoc si quisquam alius, acutissimè adstruxit deduxitque Doctissimus Gomarus, Operum Theol. Tom. 3. Disp. 35 a thesi 14. ad 20. inclusivè, in haec tandem Bellarmini verba definens: Non hic opus habemus Aristotele, cùm sensus communis sufficiat. Nam si liceat disparata de disparatis propriè affirmare, licebit eodem jure affirmare de nihilo aliquid, de aliquo nihil, de luce tenebras, de tenebris lucem, de Christo Belial, de Beliale Christum: neque fides nostra nos obligat ut defendamus quae contradictionem implicant pag. 139.
notes: Disparatum de disparato; Carlstadt out; Gomarus/Bellarmine.
